nodes.ask: Painful or swollen leg. First moves?
options: Vitals, then both legs: pulses, color, warmth, sensation, movement, skin
A D-dimer before examining the leg, to decide which patients need a scan
A venous duplex first, then the examination
A heparin infusion for presumed DVT, then the examination
nodes.chainStep: Vitals; examine both legs for pulses (handheld Doppler if impalpable), color, warmth, sensation, movement, swelling and the skin
nodes.why: The first job is the limb or life threat. Acute limb ischemia is judged at the bedside for viability, with a handheld Doppler because pulse palpation is inaccurate, and without waiting for imaging. Necrotizing infection is a clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion, edema past the redness, bullae, crepitus. For a swollen or painful leg, the history and examination look for other causes before DVT is scored, and a D-dimer comes only after the Wells score, when DVT is unlikely.

nodes.ask: Cold, pale, pulseless foot. First moves?
options: IV heparin now and an emergency vascular surgery assessment
CT angiography first; heparin once it confirms the occlusion
Aspirin and an urgent vascular clinic appointment this week

nodes.chainStep: Unfractionated heparin IV on diagnosis unless contraindicated; emergency assessment of limb viability by a clinician who can revascularize, with a handheld continuous wave Doppler; no imaging delay
nodes.why: Acute limb ischemia is an emergency. Unfractionated heparin goes in on diagnosis unless contraindicated, and a clinician able to revascularize judges viability at once, by examination and a continuous wave Doppler. Skeletal muscle tolerates ischemia for about 4 to 6 hours, and duplex, CT or MR angiography is usually unnecessary before treatment. Aspirin or a clinic slot is too little and too late.

nodes.ask: Threatened but salvageable limb. Next?
options: Revascularize now: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed lysis
Heparin alone, and reassess the limb in 24 hours to see if it recovers
Primary amputation, to avoid the injury of reperfusion
An echocardiogram for the embolic source before any procedure
nodes.chainStep: Urgent revascularization, surgical thromboembolectomy or endovascular (catheter-directed thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy); monitor for compartment syndrome and do a fasciotomy if it develops; ECG, rhythm monitoring and echo for the source, without delaying treatment
nodes.why: For a salvageable limb (categories I, IIa and IIb), revascularization, open or endovascular including catheter-directed thrombolysis, is indicated to prevent amputation, with similar limb salvage either way and more bleeding with thrombolysis; the acuity and severity of the ischemia weigh in the choice of thrombolysis, and category IIb needs revascularization immediately. Heparin alone does not reperfuse the limb, amputation is for the nonviable one, and the search for an embolic source must not delay revascularization.

Effective for occlusions under 14 days old; beyond 14 days its benefit is minimal

nodes.ask: Insensate, paralyzed foot; no arterial or venous Doppler signal. Next?
options: Amputation of the nonviable tissue, without revascularization
Catheter-directed thrombolysis, to try to save the foot
Surgical embolectomy now, with a fasciotomy at the same operation
Revascularize first, then judge which tissue has survived

nodes.why: Category III is irreversible: major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage is inevitable, and the absence of both arterial and venous Doppler signals marks a limb that may be beyond salvage. Revascularizing nonviable tissue is Class 3: Harm, because its risks outweigh any benefit and reperfusion of the ischemic metabolites can cause multiorgan failure and cardiovascular collapse.

nodes.summary: Acute limb ischemia: heparin on diagnosis and an emergency bedside assessment of viability with a Doppler; revascularize a salvageable limb and watch for compartment syndrome; amputate an irreversible one instead of reperfusing it; look for the embolic source without delaying treatment.

nodes.ask: Whole leg tense, swollen and blue. Next?
options: Admit, anticoagulate, and refer for catheter-directed thrombolysis
Home on apixaban, with the leg elevated and a clinic review in 2 days
Systemic alteplase through a peripheral vein, then heparin
An IVC filter, holding anticoagulation until it is in place
nodes.chainStep: Admit; therapeutic anticoagulation; duplex to confirm the iliofemoral DVT; urgent referral for catheter-directed (not systemic) thrombolysis if the bleeding risk is low
nodes.why: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is limb-threatening DVT: ASH places it among the DVTs better treated in hospital, and thrombolysis is reasonable to consider, catheter-directed rather than systemic when lysis is chosen. NICE adds conditions for catheter-directed thrombolysis in iliofemoral DVT: symptoms under 14 days, good functional status, life expectancy of a year or more and a low bleeding risk. An IVC filter is only for a patient who cannot be anticoagulated.

sources.where: Recommendation 1 remarks and text; recommendation 5 remarks; recommendation 8

orders.dose: The sources read name no agent for phlegmasia
orders.note: Agent choice before a procedure is not stated in ASH 2020 or NICE NG158.

orders.dose: Initial dose 5,000 units by intravenous injection; continuous 20,000 to 40,000 units/24 hours by infusion; adequate when the aPTT is 1.5 to 2 times normal (label full-dose regimen, based on a 68 kg patient)
Reasonable for limb-threatening DVT; NICE: iliofemoral DVT with symptoms under 14 days, good functional status, life expectancy 1 year or more, low bleeding risk
Catheter-directed over systemic for extensive DVT
Not unless anticoagulation is contraindicated

nodes.summary: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens: limb-threatening DVT, started in hospital with anticoagulation; catheter-directed thrombolysis is reasonable when the bleeding risk is low. Which anticoagulant, and when surgical thrombectomy fits, are not in this pathway's sources.

Shock with a painful or swollen leg: resuscitate first. A hot, red leg or fever goes to the sepsis pathway, whose skin route takes necrotizing signs straight to surgery; without infection, look for a high-risk PE in the dyspnea pathway's shock route, which starts with a bedside echo. Phlegmasia in shock also starts here.

Leg symptoms with PE symptoms: continue in the dyspnea pathway, where the two-level PE Wells score, with DVT signs worth 3 points, decides between a D-dimer and CTPA. With signs of both, NICE lets the first test be for either DVT or PE, by clinical judgment.

nodes.ask: Necrotizing signs on the leg, not in shock. Next?
options: Emergency surgical debridement and broad IV antibiotics now
CT of the leg first; operate only if it shows gas in the tissue
An LRINEC score first; operate only if the score is high
IV antibiotics now; operate if it is worse in 24 hours
nodes.chainStep: Emergency surgical consultation and debridement in the operating room as soon as possible (within 6 hours of admission, WSES 2022); blood cultures and deep tissue samples; broad antibiotics covering MRSA, gram-negatives and anaerobes, with clindamycin or linezolid (for example vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin)
nodes.why: Necrotizing infection is a clinical diagnosis, and early surgical debridement is the main determinant of outcome: WSES 2022 asks for it within 6 hours of admission, where its 2018 consensus said 12. Imaging must neither delay nor deter surgery, gas in the tissue marks advanced disease, and a low LRINEC score does not rule the diagnosis out. Antibiotics are an adjunct to debridement, never a substitute.

sources.where: NSTI diagnosis (1C, 1B, 1A); timing of source control (1B); antibiotics (1B, 1C)

orders.dose: As soon as possible: within 6 hours of admission (WSES 2022); WSES 2018 said at least within 12 hours
orders.note: The sepsis pathway quotes the 2018 figure of 12 hours.

orders.dose: Every 12 to 24 hours, sooner if worse, until little or no debridement is needed
Blood cultures, and deep tissue from the edge between healthy and necrotic tissue at the first debridement
Broad cover including MRSA and gram-negatives, with clindamycin or linezolid against toxin production

Unstable: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 h or meropenem 1 g every 8 h, plus linezolid 600 mg every 12 h or vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg load then 15 to 20 mg/kg every 8 h, plus clindamycin 600 to 900 mg every 8 h. Stable: amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2/2.2 g every 8 h, or ceftriaxone 2 g every 24 h with metronidazole 500 mg every 8 h, plus clindamycin 600 to 900 mg every 8 h

orders.dose: Avoid
With organ dysfunction: a 1 L balanced crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes and antibiotics within 1 hour; 30 mL/kg within 3 hours if hypotensive or the lactate is raised
IVIG may be considered for group A streptococcal NSTI; hyperbaric oxygen only where available and never delaying care

outcomes.if: Necrotizing; grey fascia that does not bleed, dishwater fluid
No necrosis; the fascia is healthy and bleeds

nodes.summary: Necrotizing soft tissue infection: debridement as soon as possible, re-explored every 12 to 24 hours until little or none is needed; broad antibiotics with clindamycin or linezolid until no more debridement is needed, the patient is better and the fever has settled for 48 to 72 hours, narrowed on the cultures.
No necrosis at exploration: treat as severe cellulitis with IV antibiotics and keep re-examining; a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection is treated as necrotizing from the beginning.

nodes.ask: Both legs swollen; no limb threat, no PE symptoms. Next?
options: Review the drugs; NT-proBNP, urine protein, albumin, liver tests
A loop diuretic first; tests only if the swelling persists
Antibiotics for cellulitis of both legs, then a review
Compression stockings, and a review in a month without any tests
nodes.chainStep: Medication review (calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine); NT-proBNP; urine protein quantified, with serum albumin; ECG; renal, liver and thyroid function, blood count and urinalysis
nodes.why: Symmetric swelling sends you looking for a systemic cause. NT-proBNP is measured when heart failure is suspected; diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta blockers and MRAs can lower it. For nephrotic syndrome the urine protein is quantified, with the serum albumin. Amlodipine causes edema in a dose-related way, and cellulitis is called only after non-infectious causes such as venous insufficiency are excluded.

orders.dose: Urgent specialist assessment and transthoracic echocardiography within 2 weeks
Specialist assessment and transthoracic echocardiography within 6 weeks
Heart failure less likely in an untreated person; review other causes
Quantify the proteinuria; kidney biopsy is the gold standard for glomerular disease
Edema is its most common adverse reaction and dose related: 1.8% at 2.5 mg, 3.0% at 5 mg, 10.8% at 10 mg, 0.6% on placebo
If a CCB is not tolerated because of edema, offer a thiazide-like diuretic for the hypertension instead

nodes.note: Not in this version: bilateral DVT and venous obstruction, chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema.

nodes.summary: Bilateral swelling: review the drugs and replace a CCB that causes edema (NICE: a thiazide-like diuretic); NT-proBNP for heart failure, with an echo timed by its level; quantified urine protein with albumin for nephrotic syndrome.

Pregnant, DVT possible; swollen or painful leg
Cellulitis, no MRSA risk; spreading red, warm, tender skin, no pus

Abscess; a fluctuant swelling with pus

nodes.ask: Cellulitis, no pus, no MRSA risk. Antibiotic?
options: A beta-lactam: oral cephalexin, or IV cefazolin if unwell
Oral TMP-SMX alone, the usual cover for community-acquired MRSA
IV vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam, then narrow
No antibiotic yet; elevate the leg and review in 2 days
nodes.chainStep: Oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours (NICE: flucloxacillin) for 5 days, longer if not resolved; IV cefazolin 2 g every 8 hours if systemically unwell
nodes.why: Cellulitis is treated with an antibiotic against gram-positive bacteria, streptococci above all, orally first when the patient can take it and is not severely unwell. WSES 2022 says TMP-SMX and doxycycline have no activity against group A and B streptococci, so for an MRSA risk it adds them to a beta-lactam; NICE still lists doxycycline alone for penicillin allergy. Vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam is for MRSA risk, gram-negative risk or failure, and NICE offers an antibiotic to everyone with cellulitis. NICE's first choice is flucloxacillin; WSES lists cephalexin or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

orders.dose: Cephalexin 500 mg every 6 h, or amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g every 8 h; beta-lactam allergy: clindamycin 300 mg every 8 h

orders.dose: Flucloxacillin 500 mg to 1 g four times a day; penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 500 mg twice a day, or doxycycline 200 mg on day 1 then 100 mg daily; erythromycin in pregnancy
orders.note: WSES 2022 says TMP-SMX and doxycycline have no activity against group A and B streptococci, so for an MRSA risk it adds them to a beta-lactam; NICE still lists doxycycline alone for penicillin allergy.

When adherent, without general signs of inflammation or hemodynamic instability

options: IV vancomycin if unwell; if well, cephalexin plus TMP-SMX
Oral cephalexin alone; injection drug use does not change the cover
Oral TMP-SMX alone, covering both MRSA and streptococci
Oral ciprofloxacin alone, covering skin flora and MRSA
nodes.chainStep: If systemically unwell: vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg IV load, then 15 to 20 mg/kg every 12 hours, or linezolid 600 mg every 12 hours. If well: oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours plus TMP-SMX 160/800 mg every 12 hours or doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours
nodes.why: MRSA cover is added only for a risk: injection drug use or penetrating trauma, MRSA infection or colonization in the past year, 5 days of antibiotics in the last 90, immunocompromise or critical illness, or no response to first-line treatment. TMP-SMX, doxycycline and minocycline cover MRSA but not streptococci, so they go with a beta-lactam, or clindamycin is used alone despite common resistance; fluoroquinolones are not adequate for MRSA. A systemically unwell patient gets IV vancomycin or linezolid.

Vancomycin 15 to 20 mg/kg two or three times a day (maximum 2 g a dose), adjusted to serum levels, added to a first-line antibiotic

nodes.ask: Fluctuant abscess on the leg. Next?
options: Incision and drainage; an antibiotic too if redness spreads past it
Oral antibiotics alone, and drain it only if they fail to shrink it
A warm compress to bring it to a head, and drain it next week
IV vancomycin first, and drain it once it has become smaller
nodes.chainStep: Incision and drainage, breaking up loculations, left open and lightly packed; add an antibiotic (TMP-SMX or doxycycline where MRSA is common, cephalexin otherwise) when cellulitis surrounds it, it is over 5 cm, or the patient is immunosuppressed
nodes.why: Incision and drainage is the primary treatment for an abscess, and antibiotics without drainage can leave a hard lump of sterile pus. A simple abscess, its redness confined to the abscess, needs no antibiotic; one with cellulitis around it generally gets one, aimed at S. aureus, with an MRSA agent where more than 10% of S. aureus isolates are MRSA or the patient is at high risk. WSES reports methicillin resistance in 35.9% of S. aureus from skin infections in North America. An abscess over 5 cm, at a hard-to-drain site, multiple, or in an immunosuppressed patient also earns an antibiotic.

sources.where: Superficial infections (1C) and text; MRSA in cSSTI, text

orders.dose: TMP-SMX 160/800 to 320/1600 mg every 12 h, doxycycline 100 mg every 12 h or minocycline 100 mg every 12 h
Cephalexin 500 mg every 6 h or amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g every 8 h
Vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg load, then 15 to 20 mg/kg every 12 h, or linezolid 600 mg every 12 h
5 days, extended to 7 to 10 if not resolved
Not routine; can help when immunosuppressed, severe or not responding

nodes.ask: Antibiotic chosen. What else?
options: Mark the edge, treat edema or tinea, reassess if no better in 2 to 3 days
Swab the unbroken skin and choose the antibiotic by the result
Change the antibiotic if the redness has not faded by 24 hours
Give a full 14-day course from the start, so the infection does not come back
nodes.chainStep: Draw around the redness with a single-use marker before treatment; treat edema, venous insufficiency, eczema, tinea and diabetes; reassess if worse at any point or not improving in 2 to 3 days
nodes.why: Drawing around the infection before treatment shows whether it spreads; redness is harder to see on darker skin. Predisposing conditions are treated, edema from calcium channel blockers included, and edema, venous insufficiency and tinea pedis make it recur. Skin takes time to return to normal, so the trigger to reassess is worsening, or no improvement in 2 to 3 days, not redness at 24 hours. A swab helps only when the skin is broken, and the course is 5 to 7 days unless the clinical assessment says otherwise.

nodes.ask: Pregnant, swollen tender calf. Next?
options: Compression ultrasound of the leg, including the iliac veins
A D-dimer first; scan only if it is positive
LMWH on the clinical findings; no scan in pregnancy
Contrast venography as the first test

nodes.why: ASH's pregnancy guideline builds the workup on compression ultrasound with imaging of the iliac veins, and after a negative first scan it suggests further investigation, serial compression ultrasound or MR venography, rather than none. The D-dimer is of limited use in pregnancy because it is so often positive, so it does not decide who is scanned, and treating on the clinical findings alone skips the diagnosis.

outcomes.if: DVT on ultrasound; a deep vein will not compress

nodes.summary: Initial scan negative in pregnancy: serial compression ultrasound or MR venography, not no further tests (ASH 2018 pregnancy rec 31)

nodes.ask: Pregnant, DVT confirmed on ultrasound. Anticoagulant?
options: Low molecular weight heparin, once or twice daily
Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice
Heparin with warfarin for 5 days, then warfarin
Unfractionated heparin, adjusted to the aPTT
nodes.chainStep: Therapeutic LMWH once or twice daily, without routine anti-Xa monitoring; no warfarin and no DOAC
nodes.why: In pregnancy ASH recommends LMWH over unfractionated heparin (strong), once or twice daily, without routine anti-Xa monitoring. Vitamin K antagonists cross the placenta, with teratogenicity, pregnancy loss and fetal bleeding, and the DOACs are likely to cross it with unknown effects; the apixaban label does not recommend it in pregnancy. ASH also suggests against adding catheter-directed thrombolysis for DVT in pregnancy.

1 mg/kg SC every 12 hours (label DVT dose; 1.5 mg/kg once daily is the label's inpatient alternative); ASH accepts once or twice daily

orders.dose: Not in pregnancy: vitamin K antagonists cross the placenta; DOACs likely do, effects unknown
Scheduled delivery, with therapeutic LMWH stopped beforehand
Low-risk acute VTE: start as an outpatient
Not stated for DVT in the sources read

nodes.summary: DVT in pregnancy: LMWH, once or twice daily, never warfarin or a DOAC; scheduled delivery with therapeutic LMWH stopped beforehand. The duration is not in this pathway's sources.

nodes.ask: One leg swollen or painful; not pregnant, no spreading redness. Next?
options: Two-level DVT Wells score for the clinical probability
A D-dimer first, whatever the clinical probability
Contrast venography as the first test for a clot
Treat as DVT for 3 months, without any further testing first
nodes.chainStep: Two-level DVT Wells score: 1 point each for active cancer, paralysis or a recent cast, bedridden 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, tenderness along the deep veins, whole leg swollen, calf 3 cm or more larger, pitting edema confined to that leg, collateral superficial veins, previous DVT; minus 2 if another diagnosis is as likely. 2 or more: likely
nodes.why: Suspected DVT starts with a clinical probability from a validated rule; NICE uses the two-level Wells score, 2 points or more DVT likely. The probability decides the next test: a D-dimer when DVT is unlikely, an ultrasound when it is likely, and a positive D-dimer alone diagnoses nothing. Compression ultrasound, not venography, is the first-line imaging.

orders.dose: 1 point each: active cancer; paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilization; bedridden 3 days or more or major surgery within 12 weeks; localized tenderness along the deep veins; entire leg swollen; calf at least 3 cm larger than the other side; pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg; collateral superficial veins; previously documented DVT. Minus 2: an alternative diagnosis at least as likely. 2 or more likely, 1 or less unlikely

outcomes.if: DVT unlikely; 1 point or less
DVT likely; 2 points or more

nodes.ask: DVT unlikely on Wells. Next?
options: A D-dimer, age-adjusted over 50; scan only if it is positive
Discharge now, since a low Wells score on its own rules DVT out
Anticoagulate if the D-dimer is positive, without a scan
Contrast venography as the first test
nodes.chainStep: D-dimer with the result within 4 hours (interim therapeutic anticoagulation if it will take longer); consider an age-adjusted cutoff over 50; compression ultrasound if positive
nodes.why: With DVT unlikely, a highly sensitive D-dimer comes first: a negative one rules DVT out with no further testing, and a positive one goes to ultrasound, never straight to treatment. NICE considers an age-adjusted threshold over 50. The D-dimer helps little in hospitalized, postsurgical or pregnant patients, in whom it is often positive. If it will take more than 4 hours, interim therapeutic anticoagulation covers the wait. Where a D-dimer is not readily available, ASH accepts ultrasound alone.

orders.dose: Consider for people over 50
Result within 4 hours, or interim therapeutic anticoagulation while waiting

outcomes.if: Negative; below the cutoff
Positive; above the cutoff

nodes.ask: DVT likely, or unlikely with a positive D-dimer. Next?
options: Compression ultrasound, proximal or whole leg, within 4 hours
A D-dimer first, and an ultrasound only if the D-dimer is positive
Anticoagulate for 3 months on the probability alone
Contrast venography as the first imaging test
nodes.chainStep: Compression ultrasound (proximal, or whole leg) with the result within 4 hours; if it will take longer, interim therapeutic anticoagulation and the scan within 24 hours
nodes.why: A likely Wells score, or an unlikely one with a positive D-dimer, goes to ultrasound: NICE scans the proximal leg veins, and ASH accepts proximal or whole-leg ultrasound; only a whole-leg scan also images the calf veins. When the result cannot come within 4 hours, interim anticoagulation covers the wait and the scan follows within 24 hours. A D-dimer does not decide whether a likely patient is scanned, and a probability is not a diagnosis.

orders.dose: If the scan cannot be done within 4 hours; choose one that can continue if DVT is confirmed; take a blood count, renal and liver function, PT and APTT without waiting for the results

nodes.ask: Wells likely, scan negative, no other diagnosis. Next?
options: Repeat the scan in about a week (NICE: if a D-dimer is positive)
Discharge, since one negative scan rules DVT out
Diagnose DVT on a positive D-dimer and start full anticoagulation
Treat for 3 months because the Wells score was high
nodes.chainStep: ASH: serial ultrasound, one more scan in 1 week. NICE: D-dimer; if positive, stop interim anticoagulation and repeat the proximal scan 6 to 8 days later; if negative, DVT is not likely
nodes.why: With DVT likely, one negative scan is not the end: ASH follows it with a serial scan a week later when no other diagnosis is found, and NICE checks a D-dimer, repeating the proximal scan 6 to 8 days later only if it is positive, with interim anticoagulation stopped meanwhile. A positive D-dimer alone never diagnoses DVT.

nodes.ask: Ultrasound: no DVT, a ruptured Baker cyst. Management?
options: Rest, ice, compression, elevation and an NSAID
Anticoagulate for 3 months, as for a calf DVT
Arthroscopic surgery on the knee this admission
Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the calf fluid today
nodes.chainStep: Rest, ice, a compression bandage, elevation and an NSAID or other analgesic; treat the knee; reassess for compartment syndrome if the pain and swelling escalate
nodes.why: A ruptured Baker cyst leaks synovial fluid into the calf and mimics DVT, which is why duplex comes first: it excludes DVT. Most ruptures settle with conservative care, rest, ice, compression, elevation and anti-inflammatories, most within 4 to 12 weeks. Aspiration with a steroid injection is for persistent or recurrent cases, surgery for refractory symptoms or the joint lesion behind them, and anticoagulation without a DVT is the misdiagnosis to avoid.

orders.dose: Severe pain, tense swelling, neurovascular impairment or foot drop: immediate fasciotomy

nodes.ask: Isolated distal DVT, mild symptoms, no risk factor for extension. Next?

nodes.chainStep: Repeat ultrasound over the next 2 weeks (CHEST; ESVS: a whole-leg scan at 1 week) instead of anticoagulation; anticoagulate as for proximal DVT if it reaches the proximal veins
nodes.why: For an isolated distal DVT without severe symptoms or risk factors for extension, CHEST suggests serial imaging of the deep veins for 2 weeks over anticoagulation (weak), and ESVS repeats a whole-leg scan after 1 week in an untreated patient; the scans look for progression toward the proximal veins. Anticoagulation, when chosen, is the same regimen as for proximal DVT. Thrombolysis should be rare below the common femoral vein, and an IVC filter is not offered when anticoagulation is possible.

orders.dose: Raised D-dimer without another cause, clot over 5 cm or over 7 mm or in more than one vein, close to the proximal veins, unprovoked, active cancer, previous VTE, inpatient, significant symptoms, unwilling to have repeat scans

nodes.why: ASH suggests a DOAC over a vitamin K antagonist, and NICE offers apixaban or rivaroxaban first, for at least 3 months. Neither needs a parenteral start; each begins at a higher dose instead, for 7 days with apixaban and 3 weeks with rivaroxaban, while dabigatran and edoxaban follow 5 to 10 days of heparin. Unfractionated heparin with warfarin is not routine unless renal failure or a high bleeding risk calls for it.

nodes.ask: Unprovoked DVT, 3 months of treatment done. Next?

Stop at 3 months, the same as for a provoked clot

nodes.chainStep: Continue anticoagulation indefinitely for secondary prevention when the bleeding risk allows, reviewed at least yearly; a lower-dose DOAC may be considered after the primary course
nodes.why: After an unprovoked DVT, ASH suggests indefinite antithrombotic therapy over stopping, and NICE considers continuing beyond 3 months, telling patients with a low bleeding risk that the benefits likely outweigh the risks. Prognostic scores, a D-dimer or residual clot on ultrasound are not used routinely to decide, and anticoagulation is preferred to aspirin for secondary prevention. NICE suggests discussing stopping if the HAS-BLED score is 4 or more and cannot be modified.

nodes.ask: DVT with active cancer. Anticoagulant for the first 3 to 6 months?
options: A DOAC, used carefully in GI cancers; LMWH if a DOAC is unsuitable

nodes.chainStep: Apixaban or rivaroxaban at treatment doses (or edoxaban after heparin) for 3 to 6 months, used carefully in GI cancers; LMWH if a DOAC is unsuitable; check interactions with the cancer drugs; then continue while the cancer is active
nodes.why: For the first 3 to 6 months ASH suggests a DOAC, apixaban, edoxaban or rivaroxaban, over LMWH, and either over a vitamin K antagonist; NICE considers a DOAC and turns to LMWH when a DOAC is unsuitable. DOACs are used carefully in GI cancers, where GI bleeding is more common, and tumour site, drug interactions and bleeding risk shape the choice. For the first week LMWH is recommended over unfractionated heparin, and an IVC filter is not a substitute for anticoagulation.
